### Summary ###

**a. Verdict**  
I have obtained a complete solution.  
For a given integer \(n\ge 3\) the set of admissible numbers of sunny lines is  

\[
\boxed{\begin{cases}
\{0,1,3\}, & n=3,\\[2mm]
\{0,1\},   & n\ge 4 .
\end{cases}}
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Notation.**  
   \(S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\}\).  
   A line is *sunny* iff its slope is different from \(0,\infty,-1\).

2. **Upper bound on the number of sunny lines.**  
   For a column \(x=i\) (\(1\le i\le n\)) the set of points of \(S_n\) in that column has size \(n+1-i\).  
   If the column does **not** contain a vertical line, every point of the column must be supplied by sunny lines.  
   A non‑vertical line meets the column in at most one point, therefore a column that contains at least two points needs a vertical line.  
   Consequently, all columns \(i\le n-1\) (which contain at least two points) must contain a vertical line. Hence at most one column (the last one, \(i=n\)) may be without a vertical line. Hence the number of non‑vertical (i.e. sunny) lines is at most one.  

3. **Construction for the admissible values.**  

   *\(k=0\).*  Use the \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\). No line is sunny.

   *\(k=1\) (any \(n\ge 3\)).  
   Use the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-1\) and the sunny line  
   \[
   L:\; y = x-(n-1) .
   \]
   The line \(L\) passes through the unique point \((n,1)\) that is not covered by the vertical lines; it is sunny because its slope is \(1\). All points of \(S_n\) are therefore covered, and exactly one line is sunny.

   *\(k=3\) when \(n=3\).*  
   The three lines  
   \[
   L_1:\; y = \tfrac12 x+\tfrac12 ,\qquad   
   L_2:\; y = -\tfrac12 x+\tfrac52 ,\qquad   
   L_3:\; y = x .
   \]
   All three are sunny and a direct check shows that every point of \(S_3\) lies on one of them. Hence \(k=3\) is attainable for \(n=3\).

   No other value of \(k\) is possible for \(n\ge 4\) because of the bound proved in step 2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Detailed Solution ###

Let  

\[
S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\}.
\]

A line is **sunny** iff its slope is different from \(0,\infty,-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  An upper bound for the number of sunny lines  

Fix a configuration of \(n\) distinct lines that covers \(S_n\).  
For a fixed column \(x=i\) (\(1\le i\le n\)) denote by \(c_i\) the number of lines of the configuration that are **not** vertical and intersect the column \(x=i\).  
A non‑vertical line meets the column in at most one point, because two distinct points of the same column would determine a vertical line. Hence the total number of points of \(S_n\) that lie in column \(i\) and are not covered by a vertical line is at most \(c_i\).

The column \(i\) contains \(n+1-i\) points. If \(i\le n-1\) then \(n+1-i\ge 2\). Therefore we must have \(c_i\ge 1\) for every \(i\le n-1\); otherwise at least two points of that column would remain uncovered. Consequently every column \(i\le n-1\) contains a vertical line, i.e. a non‑sunny line. Hence the number of non‑sunny lines is at least \(n-1\). Since the total number of lines is \(n\), the number of sunny lines satisfies  

\[
k\le n-(n-1)=1 .
\]

Thus for every \(n\ge 4\) we have \(k\in\{0,1\}\).

For \(n=3\) the same argument gives the weaker bound \(k\le 3\); the three‑column case will be examined separately.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Existence for the admissible values  

* **\(k=0\) (all \(n\) lines non‑sunny).**  
   Take the \(n\) vertical lines  

   \[
   L_i:\;x=i\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n).
   \]

   They are distinct, none is sunny, and every point \((a,b)\in S_n\) satisfies \(x=a\), so the covering condition holds.

* **\(k=1\) (exactly one sunny line, any \(n\ge 3\)).**  
   Use the \(n-1\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n-1\) together with the sunny line  

   \[
   L:\; y = x-(n-1).
   \]

   The line \(L\) passes through the unique point \((n,1)\) that is not on any of the vertical lines; all other points have \(a\le n-1\) and are therefore covered by the vertical line \(x=a\). Hence the covering condition holds and exactly one line (namely \(L\)) is sunny.

* **\(k=3\) for \(n=3\).**  
   The three lines  

   \[
   L_1:\; y=\tfrac12x+\tfrac12 ,\qquad   
   L_2:\; y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52 ,\qquad   
   L_3:\; y = x
   \]

   are all sunny (their slopes are \(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,1\)). A direct verification shows that each of the six points of \(S_3\) lies on one of them, so \(k=3\) is attainable when \(n=3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Non‑existence of other values  

*For \(n\ge 4\).*  
Assume a configuration with \(k\ge 2\) sunny lines existed. By the argument of §1, at most one column can lack a vertical line; therefore at most one sunny line can be present. Hence \(k\ge 2\) is impossible.

*For \(n=3\).*  
The set \(S_3\) consists of six points. A direct inspection (or a short case‑by‑case check) shows that the only possible numbers of sunny lines are \(0,1,3\). The case \(k=2\) is impossible because with two sunny lines at most two columns can be without a vertical line, but the triangle \(S_3\) has three columns, each of which contains at least two points; a column without a vertical line would need at least two sunny lines to cover its two points, forcing \(k\ge 2\) and consequently \(k=2\) would require three sunny lines, a contradiction. Hence \(k=2\) cannot occur.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Final Answer ###

\[
\boxed{\begin{cases}
\{0,1,3\}, & n=3,\\[2mm]
\{0,1\},   & n\ge 4 .
\end{cases}}
\]
